What if a humanoid could suppress a specific movement without losing the rest of the motion?

RedirectMimic introduces a local motion-content redaction method for whole-body control. It lets the policy observe the original reference while training it to follow a rule-generated edited target—replacing selected arm movements while preserving surrounding motion and keeping the deployed interfaces unchanged.

In Unitree G1 simulation, the method reduced overhead-arm content occurrence to 2.7% and achieved 94.2% core-window joint success, while maintaining tracking accuracy on unedited motions comparable to a pretrained controller. 

Title: RedirectMimic: Local Motion Content Redaction for Humanoid Whole-Body Control
Project URL: https://xiaopeng-whu.github.io/RedirectMimic/
Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14049v1

[1/4] 🚀 Introducing Infrathon (https://infrathonx.github.io/)

Can LLM agents autonomously improve real-world AI infrastructure, make new discoveries, and outperform human-designed baselines on long-horizon, open-ended optimization tasks?

AI infra optimization requires repeated implementation, profiling, and testing. Agents must preserve correctness, recover from failed experiments, and keep searching when early attempts stall. Existing evaluations often focus on specific components or shorter runs.

Together with @uwnlp, @allen_ai, @radixark, and @PyromindHS, we introduce Infrathon: a benchmark of 25 real-world, open-ended AI infrastructure optimization tasks spanning operators, modules, and end-to-end training or serving workflows, with 12–24-hour budgets.

One example: Claude Opus 5.5 increases mean KV-cache compression from 6.82× to 19.86× while improving video quality.

AI automation is more than connecting tools and running workflows.

A powerful automation system needs triggers, integrations, data processing, decision-making, execution, security, and continuous improvement.

Here are 10 essential components that make AI automation systems work.

1. Workflow Triggers — Start the Process

Triggers initiate workflows automatically.

- Time-based triggers.
- Event-based triggers.
- User-defined conditions.

2. Integration Layer — Connect Everything

Connect different applications and services using APIs and webhooks.

3. Data Ingestion — Collect Information

Gather and prepare data through three important steps:

- Clean data.
- Normalize information.
- Enrich records.

4. Data Transformation — Prepare Raw Data

Convert collected information into structured, usable data for automation and decision-making.

5. AI Decision Engine — Make Smarter Decisions

Three approaches power automated decisions:

- Rule-based logic.
- Learning-based models.
- Agentic AI.

6. Workflow Orchestration — Coordinate Tasks

Manage task sequencing, dependencies, and worker queues to keep workflows organized.

7. Action Execution — Get Things Done

Execute actions such as updating databases, calling APIs, and sending notifications.

8. Performance Optimization — Improve Efficiency

Use failover mechanisms, caching, parallel execution, and human-in-the-loop controls.

9. Scalability Layer — Handle Growing Workloads

Design systems that can handle increasing tasks, users, and data without losing reliability.

10. Feedback Loop — Continuously Improve

Track execution results, outcomes, and performance metrics to improve future workflows.

- Security & Governance: Manage API keys, permissions, OAuth, and compliance.
- API Security: Ensure authentication, authorization, and access control.
- Monitoring & Reliability: Track logs, failures, audit trails, and recovery.

The real power of AI automation comes from combining all these components into one reliable, continuously improving system.

Building multi-agent AI systems isn't just about connecting multiple LLMs.

It's about choosing the right architecture to balance cost, performance, scalability, and reliability.

Here are 6 important multi-agent design patterns every AI builder should understand.

𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘’𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗞𝗗𝗢𝗪𝗡:

01 — 𝗦𝗘𝗤𝗨𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗔𝗟 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Agents complete tasks one after another in a fixed sequence.

→ Task 1 → Task 2 → Task 3 → Output

→ Best For: Deterministic workflows with clear dependencies.

→ Cost: $

→ Hidden Cost: Slower execution when tasks could run in parallel.

→ Use When: Simplicity and reliability are priorities.

02 — 𝗣𝗔𝗥𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗘𝗟 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Multiple agents work on independent tasks simultaneously.

→ Agent A: Handles Task A.

→ Agent B: Handles Task B.

→ Agent C: Handles Task C.

→ Merge: Combines all results.

→ Best For: Reducing latency for independent tasks.

→ Cost: $$

→ Hidden Cost: Higher token usage and infrastructure costs.

→ Avoid When: Tasks depend heavily on each other.

03 — 𝗛𝗜𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗥𝗖𝗛𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

A manager agent delegates tasks to specialized agents.

→ Research Agent: Collects information.

→ Analysis Agent: Evaluates findings.

→ Data Agent: Processes data.

→ Report Agent: Generates reports.

→ Best For: Enterprise-scale workflows.

→ Cost: $$$

→ Hidden Cost: Complex orchestration and higher development effort.

→ Long-Term Value: Reusable sub-agents create leverage across workflows.

04 — 𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗢𝗥–𝗖𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗖 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

One agent generates an output while another reviews and improves it.

→ Generator Agent: Creates the initial output.

→ Critic Agent: Reviews quality and identifies issues.

→ Revision: Improves the generated result.

→ Best For: Content, code, plans, and complex outputs.

→ Cost: $$$

→ Hidden Cost: Multiple inference loops increase latency and cost.

→ Worth It When: Accuracy matters more than speed.

05 — 𝗛𝗨𝗠𝗔𝗡-𝗜𝗡-𝗧𝗛𝗘-𝗟𝗢𝗢𝗣

AI performs tasks while humans review important decisions.

→ AI Agent: Processes the request.

→ Human Review: Checks the result.

→ Action: Executes the approved task.

→ Feedback: Improves future execution.

→ Best For: High-risk decisions and compliance workflows.

→ Cost: $$$

→ Hidden Cost: Manual effort and additional latency.

→ Essential For: Legal, safety, billing, and critical decisions.

06 — 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗢𝗦𝗜𝗧𝗘 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Combines multiple design patterns into one complex workflow.

→ Sequential: Executes dependent tasks.

→ Parallel: Handles independent tasks.

→ Hierarchical: Delegates responsibilities.

→ Generator–Critic: Reviews outputs.

→ Human-in-the-Loop: Adds human approval.

→ Best For: Complex end-to-end automation.

→ Cost: $$$$

→ Hidden Cost: High infrastructure and orchestration overhead.

→ Biggest Mistake: Using it for problems that don't need this complexity.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗗𝗨𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗖𝗞:

𝗠𝗖𝗣 — 𝗧𝗢𝗢𝗟 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗡𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗜𝗧𝗬 𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥

𝗔𝟮𝗔 — 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗖𝗢𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥

Enables different AI agents to communicate and collaborate.

→ Agent Messaging
→ Task Delegation
→ Shared Memory
→ Workflow Coordination

More agents don't automatically mean better results.

The right architecture depends on task complexity, budget, execution speed, and reliability requirements.

Start simple. Add orchestration and specialized agents only when they deliver measurable value.
